I wouldn't want to go too many months without reliving the experience of traveling to Ghana to attend a wedding. Ghana is a West African country, a semi-presidential republic. It borders Burkina Faso to the north, Togo to the east, Côte d'Ivoire to the west, and the Gulf of Guinea to the south. The territory has seen constant expeditions by Europeans, mainly Portuguese, British, and Dutch, for trading the abundant gold found throughout the area. Hence, the area was dubbed the 'Gold Coast.'

Currently, the country is one of the most powerful democracies on the continent.
We were invited to the wedding of a friend of my wife's whom she met during her university years. He lives and works in London despite being a native of Ghana, so we always thought that when he decided to take the plunge, we would make a quick trip to the UK, which is always appealing. The surprise was that he was getting married in his homeland because the bride's family and friends are largely in Ghana, and he cannot refuse his future wife's wish.

His name is Derek, and I like him a lot. I don't know him deeply, but from just a few conversations with him, you can tell he is a hard worker, very hard-working, with clear ideas and very specific goals. He works and strives to achieve those goals, and that is something I admire in anyone. In his case, his goals are what some modern types might call 'old-fashioned' or 'old-fashioned,' namely, marrying a good woman, starting a large family, and living the life our parents lived. For this, he has studied a complex career and obtained a doctorate, works more hours than a clock, and thanks God for being able to work them.

Despite not agreeing with some of his moral values, I have deep respect for the authenticity of his attitudes. He doesn't deceive anyone, nor does he deceive himself. And being like that, doing things for the right reasons, all you can do is tip your hat and observe a practical case of how to achieve happiness through different paths. His is different from mine, but authentic and functional. I am sure they will be very happy together and will have a large family as they both desire.

When we found out about the invitation, we learned from another close friend of his that Derek had hesitated to invite my wife, his friend, because he was somewhat afraid that I, her partner (her man), 'wouldn't let her go.' That's his upbringing, and those are the values that govern his life. It surprised me, someone who has spent so many years in the UK, in a big city, with so much education, working with companies from many countries... So I began to take an interest in Ghanaian culture.

In Ghana, the majority of the population practices Christianity, mainly in its Protestant and Presbyterian branches. From a young age, they study in school and imbibe the worship in their families. They are very religious. However, they lean towards Protestantism, a branch I am not very familiar with, so the trip was very enriching in that sense.

The first sensation I remember is heat. A lot of heat. Actually, it's not that bad; you get used to it in a day, but we traveled in January, in the middle of the peak cold in Barcelona. What affected us was the radical change in a few hours, from sleeping in cold weather with a duvet and long-sleeved pajamas to an average of forty-three degrees in the shade. The first breaths of air you take in Africa are fiery. Stepping off the plane, you look at the horizon and see that red sand haze, take a breath, and suddenly become very aware of your own breathing because your lungs burn. I remember how the people around me quickly got moving, accustomed to the place, standing in the queues where they should, without a minute to spare. In contrast, I asked for a few minutes to get used to it, to know where I am. Look around and understand that I'm not in a different country; I'm in another world, with its own law of gravity, with its rhythm that has nothing to do with mine.

Time presses on, and I head passport in hand following the mass hoping to receive my tourist visa. I find myself in a long line in a building that, by its structure and characteristics, reminds me of a school from the 1980s, waiting for my turn for a military (rifle on shoulder) to inspect my passport, visa papers, photograph, and face.

I pass without any problem, retrieve my suitcase, and head to the taxi exit where a crowd of people are waiting to persuade us to use their taxi. Their English has a very strong, very recognizable accent, but they are perfectly understandable. They study English at school (it is the official language of the country) and speak a couple of African dialects. They communicate among themselves in English or in their languages indifferently or with some distinction that escapes me.

In our case, a taxi driver who works for Derek's family awaits us, arriving only a few minutes late. Those minutes are enough for us to doubt, and the formidable vendors who approach us get closer and closer to their goal of tricking us into giving them a few bills. They even seem to be in league with one of the military personnel who I assume is ensuring the security of the premises, who, with his green beret, invites us to use their services, recommends one of them, tells us to wait a second, to accompany him. We look at each other, overwhelmed by the situation and the imposing nature of his attire, and above all his rifle, we begin to walk in his direction where he waits with clear gestures of "let's go, what are you waiting for?" At that moment, Mister Okaine (which is what our dear taxi driver is called) appears and identifies us immediately. In retrospect, it shouldn't have been hard for him to identify four young white people, especially when surrounded by a throng of people waving their arms and shouting to be heard over the others, almost letting us be taken away by the mysterious military man.

When he identifies himself, we interpret it as salvation, we introduce ourselves quickly, and we surrender to the expression of kindness and understanding that floods his face. At that moment, we would have trusted him to take us wherever he wanted, to the end of the world (or to its beginning), which shouldn't be very far away.

Already in his taxi, we head to the house that Derek, very kindly, has reserved for his friends heading to the wedding from Europe. It is actually a house that his father owns, which he uses for guests.

I remember the taxi ride with special fondness; at that moment, I said to myself, "look out the window well, you will never forget this moment." By that time, the sun was already setting, and soon the sky darkened completely. I remember the people on the roadside in front of shops made of adobe, sheet metal, and asbestos; they sell all kinds of junk and food. Water, especially water. It smells like food, sand, healthy. I expected a strong contrast of smells but the immense open spaces heal the wounds left by the combinations of smells in the environment.

Upon arrival at the house, we meet the other European guests, all within the same age group and of different nationalities. In total, there are Catalans, Bulgarians, English, Swedes, Italians, and Japanese. All of this adds up to a total of only eight people. After chatting with them for a while, I quickly realize that they lead lives similar to Derek's: highly educated, responsible, well-born... I'm sure I can learn a lot from them, I tell myself. And I wasn't wrong.

It's always a challenge to place two adults trying to sleep in a double inflatable bed, but if you add stifling heat, the mosquito net that wraps every inch of our space, and the loud chants of church prayers at full volume, it becomes a titanic task. Yes, religious chants, loud and vehement, all night long. With deep and grave voices, intermittently. It only happened that night; later, I learned that Mister Okaine's family (who live in an annex to the house) was celebrating some kind of religious celebration that lasts all night long. The truth is, we didn't hear it again, but to start with, it's not bad at all.

The next day, I go down to have breakfast, and far from staying in the kitchen with the rest, I go out to the patio and approach the annex where Mister Okaine's family lives as caretakers of the house. I find two children sitting on typical African stools (family members) that they have made themselves, they tell me, and they invite me to sit on one of them. At first, they are a bit distant, but they look at me and smile, like someone looking at something exotic seen on television. After a while, we start a conversation, and I ask them if they go to school; they tell me yes, that they are on vacation now. I keep asking if they like to study, what they want to be when they grow up. And they answer yes, that they have a good time, one wants to be an economist, and the girl can't quite remember what she replied.

Little by little, they start opening up and talk to me about their garden, their chickens (that run around in front of us), and the trees and plants right in front of us. They invite me to see them up close, to touch the leaves. I realize later, after being soaked in sweat by nine in the morning, that they have been walking along small strips of shade that I suppose they must recognize with their eyes closed, whereas I have been moving randomly, like an elephant in a china shop.

It's the wedding day so we have to start getting ready. It's quite an experience posing in front of a palm tree at noon (an African noon) in a long-sleeved shirt, suit, tie, and all the attire of a well-dressed gentleman, to take a few photos. The serious faces are priceless.

The wedding takes place in a sort of tent on the outskirts of the city, beautifully decorated, and aims to accommodate no more and no less than three hundred guests. We arrive early, take our seats at the back, and the choir rehearses in the background.

The ceremony begins officiated by a pastor who seems straight out of Hollywood movies and delivers, in my opinion, a very inspiring and enjoyable sermon. The bride and groom, seated at the altar, listen devoutly to her words while guests take photographs and sing hymns passionately when prompted. We do what we can, reading the lyrics and humming along from the second chorus onwards.

At one point, the pastor performed a ritual that I really liked, which involved filling a large, wide cup with fine white sand, representing God; onto which the bride and groom poured sand of different colors, symbolizing that the foundation of their union is based on God. It was a very beautiful moment, and you can always use the resulting cup to decorate the living room and have a story to tell.

Soon after, we moved to the area where the reception would take place, which was a kind of school or institute. We settled into our seats, and the newlyweds entered dancing to the rhythm of African songs escorted by their bridesmaids and groomsmen. From there, the celebration took on a casual tone that surprised me a bit, but like everything casual, it was embraced as normal. The parents of the bride danced with each other (the bride's father dressed in traditional African clothes like many of the guests), the music played loudly, and the atmosphere relaxed. Happiness was palpable, and everyone was very pleased with the union, which was conveyed throughout the room. Needless to say, being the only eight white people at the wedding (and I would say in the country, because I don't remember seeing a single white person) made us the life of the party, and the MC constantly encouraged us to liven up the evening with shouts of 'let the whites come out and dance'. Our dear Aki, Derek's Japanese friend, surprised us all with such exuberance and confidence that it left everyone stunned, coaxing middle-aged couples onto the dance floor with endless energy.

The next day, very early in the morning, we caught our flight back home and reviewed during the flight hours the experiences we had, the excellent company, and the wonderful smiles that accompanied us all the way. I wouldn't want to conclude without remembering Derek, Fiona, Maya, Xavi, Oskar, Aki, Alexandro, and Jody, our dear adventure companions who shared moments of happiness, nervousness, joys, and sorrows with us.

I went to Africa vaccinated against yellow fever and returned vaccinated against the asphalt.
